How we decide

For each everyday thing, the lexicon recommends one Latin word and shows the others. These are the rules behind those choices. Our rulings on particular words and rules are on a page of their own, each with its evidence, its date and who made it. Any of them can be reopened: if you think we got one wrong, tell us why.

The rulesNotesSourcesRulings ({{ruling_count}})

The rules

  1. Classical first. A word that classical authors use in the sense we need comes first. A post-classical word fills a real gap and must be well attested; Christian Latin is the natural source for church life (benedīcere). A coinage comes last, and a coinage of our own is labelled as ours.
  2. Source order. For modern things we consult Traupman’s Conversational Latin, then the Morgan–Owens Neo-Latin lexicon, then Levi and Bini’s Il latino come lingua viva (1937), whose words we check in Lewis & Short because it cites no sources, then the Vatican’s Lexicon Recentis Latinitatis and other modern lexica. On Latinity, classical usage outranks them all, and Smith & Hall and Morgan–Owens outrank Traupman: the chimney is camīnus, not Traupman’s fūmārium.
  3. Show every form. Where the sources differ, every form appears, the recommended one first, each labelled with its period: classical, late, medieval, Renaissance, modern, or ours.
  4. Our own words are marked. Where no source has a word, we make one: a plain classical word stretched in an obvious way (replēre, “fill up again”, for charging a phone), or a short regular formation (replētrum, a charger). Every such form carries an asterisk, *replētrum, the sign linguists use for a form that is not attested, so that it can be told at a glance from a word with a source.
  5. No word is an answer too. Where Latin has no equivalent (respectively, the), the entry says so and shows what Latin does instead.
  6. Flag false friends. A modern form that meant something else in antiquity is listed with the reason it is not used.
  7. Label register. Words that are chiefly comic, poetic or colloquial say so.
  8. Vowel length. Macrons are part of the spelling, so every long vowel is marked. Our authorities, in order: Lewis & Short; Bennett for hidden quantities that Lewis & Short leaves unmarked; and de Vaan’s Etymological Dictionary of Latin wherever he discusses the vowel. A vowel we cannot settle stays unmarked, and the entry says so.
  9. Spelling. Consonantal i is written j (jam, ejus, conjungō). Search ignores the difference, and ignores macrons too.
  10. Examples. Every example sentence is marked either as a quotation, with its source, or as composed by us.
  11. Review. Every change is checked automatically for its format, its links and its spelling of j. Entries drafted with machine help stay marked as drafts until a person has reviewed them.

Notes

Wherever an entry departs from Lewis & Short or from one of its sources, a numbered note gives the reason and the evidence. A note that rests on one of our rulings links to it. The notes are there so that you can check our reasoning, and so that we can trace a mistake to the decision that caused it.

How to read the sources

Every entry ends with its sources: the dictionaries, word lists and texts it rests on, each cited as a book cites it. What is true of all of them is said here, once.

  • “Lewis & Short” after a quotation. A quotation or a reference marked Lewis & Short is given as Lewis & Short’s dictionary cites it, with the dictionary’s reference, in our spelling (macrons, consonantal j). It has not been checked against a modern edition.
  • “Composed”. An example marked composed is a sentence of ours, not an author’s. The descriptions and prompts marked as ours were likewise composed for conversation in a family, with a child.
  • Quotations with an author’s reference. A quotation without either mark is checked against a text of its author and given in our spelling; where that was not done, the entry’s own sources say so. Many come from our own collections of quotations by author (the Latinitas loci collections) and from two notes kept with them, on words of quantity and on suppletive verbs; each collection names the edition its quotations were checked against, or, for Vives, the transcription. Prayers come from the collection of prayers kept beside them, the Precēs, checked against the sources it names. The quotations that are not in Lewis & Short or in those collections were checked against the Perseus Latin texts (the Perseus Digital Library’s canonical-latinLit) or the Latin Library texts (the CLTK’s mirror), on 9, 11 and 12 November 2026.
  • Editions and numbering. The Perseus texts are these editions: Plautus, Leo (1896), cited by his line numbers; Terence, Parry (1857), cited by the lines of the Oxford text, from which Parry’s can run one off (lines taken from the loci collections are cited by the Oxford text’s too); Cicero’s letters, Purser, with his sections; De oratore, Wilkins; the Tusculans, Pohlenz; De officiis, Miller; De natura deorum, Plasberg; the Philippics, Clark; Caesar, Rice Holmes (1914); Vergil, Greenough (1881); Horace, Fairclough (1929); Pliny’s Natural History, Mayhoff (Teubner, 1906), read in the Perseus Digital Library, with his section numbers. Quintilian is cited by the numbering of the Perseus text. Some passages checked against the Latin Library’s text take their section numbers from the Perseus text; the Latin Library’s Terence follows the Oxford text. For the names of places, ancient passages that Lewis & Short does not quote were read in the Latin Library’s texts (thelatinlibrary.com), in a copy kept here, and are cited by book and section.
  • The Vulgate. Verses are quoted from the Clementine Vulgate, in its spelling, and cited by book, chapter and verse. They were checked against the CrossWire VulgClementine text, through the scrollmapper bible_databases repository (the text our collection of Vulgate quotations uses), and against Hetzenauer’s edition; a few against the Clementine text at Bible Study Tools and the Latin Library’s text. For the names of places the Vulgate was read in the Latin Library’s text.
  • Publilius Syrus. He is cited as our collection numbers him: by position under each initial letter in the Latin Library’s text. From N onwards that numbering differs from Meyer’s. “Ps.-Publil.” marks lines from the later collections printed with him.
  • The reference works. Beside a word, Traupman’s Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency is cited by its printed page (“Traupman 103”), Morgan–Owens by headword (“M-O s.v. sieve”), with the authorities it cites, Levi and Bini by printed page (“Levi–Bini p. 23”), Andresian’s Vocabula Picta by printed page (“Andresian p. 24”), and Graesse by headword (“Graesse, Orbis Latinus s.v.”). Under Sources each work has one line, with all its pages.
  • Graesse’s Orbis Latinus. The names of places are taken from two editions: Benedict’s of 1909, Latin–German, read in the digitisation at columbia.edu, and that of Dresden 1861, in its German–Latin index, read in the scan at archive.org. Where the 1909 edition could not be reached page by page, the 1861 edition stands alone; where an entry cites both, the 1861 edition is cited only for what differs. Graesse’s forms are post-classical unless Lewis & Short has them.
  • Links to a dictionary. A link to a dictionary article supports the word it names. Where an entry gives a modern expression built from such words, or a sentence of ours that uses them, the link documents the words, not the expression or the sentence; those are marked as ours. A word recorded here for a modern or technical thing, in computing or climbing as anywhere else, is not thereby a settled technical standard.

Rulings

A ruling is a recorded decision: a rule for many words, or a choice on one word where we depart from a dictionary or a source. All {{ruling_count}} are on the rulings page, with their evidence, history and the words that cite them.
